description: Mobile Hacking Community talks from DEF CON 34.

talks.title: A Droidwork Orange - A Longitudinal Study of Android Security Research
talks.teaser: Presents a longitudinal study of Android security papers from 2008 to 2025, tracing shifts in topics, contributors, publication venues and platform influence.
talks.summary:
The talk asks how Android security research has changed since the first related paper appeared in 2009, and whether the recent drop in publication volume means the field is exhausted or mature. The authors pulled paper metadata from Scopus, including titles, abstracts, keywords and affiliations, and built a corpus they call Ludovico. They removed false positives through repeated rounds of BERTopic clustering and manual review. They ran the same process on iOS papers and surveyed researchers to compare the literature with their own views.

Output rose until a peak around 2016 to 2018 and then fell. App privacy and security led the early literature, but malware detection overtook it and has dominated since 2017. The share of AI-based work grew sharply from 2020, and most of it targets malware detection. Academia produced the large majority of papers, with industry contributing little, and conference output declined while journal output stayed steady. Where Google standardized a feature, such as runtime permissions or biometric authentication, research interest in that topic tended to fade. On iOS, digital forensics is the leading topic.

The speakers argue that the field is maturing rather than disappearing. Most surveyed researchers said Android security is not solved. Their advice is that progress now needs low-level expertise in the kernel, the trusted execution environment and native code, real physical devices rather than only emulators, and fresher malware datasets.

talks.title: IsMyPhonePwned
talks.teaser: Presents IsMyPhonePwned, an open-source framework that scans Android and iOS phones for compromise indicators from a browser over USB, without rooting or installing software.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a practical gap: when a phone may be running spyware, investigators need a quick way to judge whether it is compromised. Traditional forensic workflows can be destructive, can break access to critical apps, and require expensive workstations, so journalists, rights groups, and corporate incident responders often have no fast option. The speaker explains the two system logs that matter most, the Android bug report and the iOS sysdiagnose archive, and how each can be collected manually, through ADB, or through commercial mobile management products that may send the data to a vendor's servers.

The main part of the talk covers IsMyPhonePwned. Its browser front end connects to a phone over USB, generates or retrieves the log, and parses it client-side using a Rust codebase compiled to WebAssembly, so nothing leaves the browser. Matching is done with rule sets from Amnesty International and with Sigma rules. The speaker also shows a Samsung patch-status tool for fleet management, an ADB-based path with YARA scanning, and a self-hosted backend built on ClickHouse for hunting across many cases. Linux was the tested platform, and the speaker noted that Chrome works best.

The closing message is that these logs hold sensitive personal and location data, so organizations should know where any collected log is stored before they adopt a triage tool. The tools are meant for fast, non-destructive triage at scale, with deeper investigation reserved for devices that look bad.
